records.complete_line: The gaps trap is positivised exclusion. A humanity defined by what AI cannot do is a "me" constituted wholly by its not-me: the distinction selects, and then the human pole claims the whole economy of encounter as its property. The domain shrinks by another's progress because the identity was borrowed from the boundary rather than from any ground of its own. The not-me is admitted only as for-me, as resource, threat or rival. At population scale, Bratton describes nativist tropes mobilized "on behalf of 'Team Human'" to redraw "new artificial boundaries of inclusion and exclusion from core social contracts" (PDF p. 46, §9.7). Bratton’s research question 14 asks how xenophobic responses arise from partial identification: xenophobic responses "rest on a problematic partial identification of self with other, such that the other is imagined as usurper" (PDF p. 57, Q14). A partial identification — not none — is the operative condition: the other must first be drawn close enough to mirror, then bounded hard enough to expel.

Bratton describes [institutional intelligence](../sources/media-technology-philosophy/bratton/bratton-2026-agentworld-brief/SOURCE.md#bratton-2026-agentworld-brief-q026) as follows: "the intelligence that makes institutions effective is not reducible to the intelligence of the agents who populate them".
